---
title: Setting up a blog
---

By the end of this chapter you will have a blog of your own, on the internet,
at an address you can send to somebody.

We are not going to write HTML by hand for every page. Instead we will use
**Jekyll**, a program that takes a folder of plain text files and turns it into
a website - one HTML page per post, with a home page listing them all. You
write in your editor, Jekyll does the rest.

The whole loop is four steps, and this chapter is those four steps in order:

1. **Set up** a blog on your own machine, with `jekyll new`.
2. **Edit** it - write a post, change the title - with `nano`.
3. **Preview** it locally, in your browser, before anyone else sees it.
4. **Build** it into a folder of plain HTML, and **copy** that to the course
   server with `scp`.

The first three happen entirely on your own computer. Nothing is public until
step four, so you can experiment freely.

## Installing Jekyll

Jekyll is written in a language called Ruby, and Ubuntu packages it for us. It
is an `apt install` like the ones in the
[Installing Software](installing-software.qmd) chapter, with two packages
named:

```session
$ sudo apt update
$ sudo apt install jekyll jekyll-theme-minima
```

The first is Jekyll itself. The second is a **theme** - the design a Jekyll
site uses unless you tell it otherwise. Jekyll's new sites expect it, so we
install both together.

That pulls in a good number of Ruby packages and takes a few minutes. Answer
`y` when it asks. When it finishes, check:

```session
$ which jekyll
/usr/bin/jekyll

$ jekyll --version
jekyll 4.3.4
```

Your version may be different from the one printed here. Anything from 3.9
onwards will do for this chapter.

## Making a blog

`jekyll new` makes a new blog. Go to your home directory and ask for one:

```session
$ cd
$ jekyll new website --skip-bundle
New jekyll site installed in /home/anand/website.
```

Look at what it made:

```session
$ cd website
$ ls
404.html  Gemfile  _config.yml  _posts  about.markdown  index.markdown
```

Each one has a job:

* `_config.yml` - the settings for the whole site: its title, your name, your
  email.
* `_posts` - the blog posts. One file per post.
* `index.markdown` - the home page.
* `about.markdown` - the about page.
* `Gemfile`, `404.html` - the machinery. Leave them alone.

The two files ending in `.markdown` are written in **Markdown**, a way of
writing formatted text as plain text. A line starting with `#` is a heading,
`*` at the start of a line makes a bullet point, and `**word**` makes a word
bold. That is most of it.

There is already one post in `_posts`:

```session
$ ls _posts
2026-08-31-welcome-to-jekyll.markdown
```

## Previewing it

Before changing anything, let's see what we have. `jekyll serve` builds the
site and then runs a small web server on your own machine so you can look at
it:

```session
$ jekyll serve
Configuration file: /home/anand/website/_config.yml
            Source: /home/anand/website
       Destination: /home/anand/website/_site
 Auto-regeneration: enabled for '/home/anand/website'
    Server address: http://127.0.0.1:4000/
  Server running... press ctrl-c to stop.
```

Open <http://127.0.0.1:4000/> in your browser. There is your blog, with the one
post Jekyll wrote for you.

Two things to notice.

The prompt has not come back. `jekyll serve` keeps running until you stop it -
that is what a server does. To stop it, press **Ctrl-C**. To carry on working
while it runs, open a second terminal.

And `Auto-regeneration: enabled`. Jekyll is watching the folder. Edit a file
and save it, and it rebuilds by itself - you only have to reload the browser.

::: {.callout-note}
`127.0.0.1` is your own computer, always. This preview is not on the internet;
nobody else can open that address. Publishing is step four.
:::

## Writing a post

A post is one file in `_posts`, and its name matters. It has to be

```
YYYY-MM-DD-some-title.markdown
```

- the date, then a short name, joined by dashes. Jekyll reads the date out of
the filename.

Let's write one. Use today's date:

```session
$ nano _posts/2026-08-31-my-first-post.markdown
```

Type this in:

```{.markdown filename="_posts/2026-08-31-my-first-post.markdown"}
---
layout: post
title: "My First Post"
date: 2026-08-31 10:00:00 +0530
---

I have a blog now.

I made it from the command line, with a program called Jekyll. These are
the commands I used:

* `jekyll new website` to make it
* `jekyll serve` to look at it
* `scp` to put it on the internet

More soon.
```

Save with **Ctrl-O**, Enter, and leave `nano` with **Ctrl-X**.

The part between the two `---` lines is the **front matter**: information about
the post rather than the post itself. `title` is what appears as the heading
and in the list on the home page. `layout: post` tells Jekyll to wrap it in the
usual page design. Every post needs those lines.

Below the second `---` is the post, in Markdown.

If `jekyll serve` is still running, reload the browser - your post is on the
home page. If you stopped it, start it again.

## Changing the title of the blog

The site still says "Your awesome title". That, and a few other things, live in
`_config.yml`:

```session
$ nano _config.yml
```

Find these lines near the top and change them:

```{.yaml filename="_config.yml"}
title: Anand's Blog
email: anand@example.com
description: >-
  Notes from the Craft of Computing course, and whatever else
  I feel like writing about.
```

::: {.callout-warning}
`_config.yml` is the one file Jekyll does *not* re-read while it is running.
After editing it, stop `jekyll serve` with Ctrl-C and start it again.
:::

While you are here, open `about.markdown` and replace the text with something
about yourself. It is your blog.

## Building the site

`jekyll serve` was for you. To publish, we need the site as ordinary files that
any web server can hand out. That is `jekyll build`:

```session
$ jekyll build
Configuration file: /home/anand/website/_config.yml
            Source: /home/anand/website
       Destination: /home/anand/website/_site
      Generating...
                    done in 0.51 seconds.
```

Everything it made is in a directory called `_site`:

```session
$ ls _site
404.html  about  assets  feed.xml  index.html  jekyll  
```

```session
$ ls _site/jekyll/2026/08/31/
my-first-post.html
```

There it is: your Markdown post, turned into an HTML page. Nothing in `_site`
is special - it is plain HTML and CSS, the same as any other web page. That is
the folder we are going to copy to the server.

::: {.callout-note}
Never edit anything inside `_site`. Jekyll deletes and rewrites it on every
build. Edit the Markdown files; let Jekyll make the HTML.
:::

## Telling Jekyll where it will live

One thing to fix before publishing. On the server your blog will not be at the
top of the site - it will be under your username, at

```
https://coc.apucomputing.com/~anand/
```

Jekyll does not know that, so the links it writes in the HTML point at `/about`
instead of `/~anand/about`, and the page comes out without its styling. Tell it
by adding a `baseurl` in `_config.yml`:

```{.yaml filename="_config.yml"}
baseurl: "/~anand"
url: "https://coc.apucomputing.com"
```

Use *your* username, not `anand`, and note the leading `/` with no trailing
one.

Then build again:

```session
$ jekyll build
```

::: {.callout-tip}
With `baseurl` set, the local preview moves too - it is now at
<http://127.0.0.1:4000/~anand/> rather than the bare address. Jekyll prints the
right one when it starts; read the `Server address:` line.
:::

## Copying it to the server

You have an account on the course server, `coc.apucomputing.com`, and a
directory in it called `public_html`. Whatever is in `public_html` is on the
web. That is the whole arrangement.

The command to copy files to another machine is `scp` - "secure copy". It is
`cp`, with one end of the copy on a different computer. A remote place is
written as

```
username@machine:path
```

Let's try it. From inside your `blog` directory:

```session
$ scp -r _site/* anand@coc.apucomputing.com:public_html/
index.html                             100% 4148    68.2KB/s   00:00
about/index.html                       100% 3721    59.4KB/s   00:00
assets/main.css                        100%   22KB  310.1KB/s   00:00
feed.xml                               100% 1102    18.9KB/s   00:00
jekyll/2026/08/31/my-first-post.html   100% 4396    71.3KB/s   00:00
```

Reading that command from the left:

* `scp` - copy, to or from another machine.
* `-r` - recursive; copy directories and everything inside them, the same `-r`
  we used with `cp` and `rm`. `_site` has directories in it, so we need it.
* `_site/*` - the contents of `_site`. The wildcard matters: `_site/*` copies
  the files *inside*, while `_site` would copy the folder itself and you would
  end up with `public_html/_site/index.html`.
* `anand@coc.apucomputing.com:public_html/` - the destination. Your username,
  the machine, a colon, and where to put it. `public_html/` is relative to your
  home directory on the server.

The first time you connect it will ask:

```
The authenticity of host 'coc.apucomputing.com' can't be established.
ED25519 key fingerprint is SHA256:4mZ8...
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])? yes
```

Type `yes` and Enter. It asks once, ever.

Now open your blog:

```
https://coc.apucomputing.com/~anand/
```

That is a page on the internet, made by you, from a terminal.

## Doing it again

The four steps only look long the first time. From now on, publishing a new
post is this:

```session
$ cd ~/website
$ nano _posts/2026-09-07-second-post.markdown
$ jekyll serve
```

Read it in the browser, fix what you do not like, stop the server with Ctrl-C,
and then:

```session
$ jekyll build
$ scp -r _site/* anand@coc.apucomputing.com:public_html/
```

Write, look, build, copy.

::: {.callout-tip}
Two commands, always in that order, and one is easy to forget. If you `scp`
without `jekyll build`, you have copied the *previous* build and your new post
is not there. If the website does not show what the preview showed, that is
almost always why.
:::

## Looking around the server

`scp` copies files. To get a shell *on* the server - to look around, or to fix
something in place - use `ssh`:

```session
$ ssh anand@coc.apucomputing.com
anand@coc:~$
```

The prompt changes, and every command you now type runs on the server, not on
your machine. Everything from the earlier chapters works there:

```session
anand@coc:~$ ls public_html
404.html  about  assets  feed.xml  index.html  jekyll

anand@coc:~$ ls -l public_html/index.html
-rw-r--r-- 1 anand anand 4148 Aug 31 10:24 public_html/index.html
```

`exit` brings you back to your own machine.

```session
anand@coc:~$ exit
logout
Connection to coc.apucomputing.com closed.
$
```

It is the same skill you have been practising all along, applied to a computer
in a data centre somewhere rather than the one in front of you. That is most of
what running a server is.

## Summary

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `sudo apt install jekyll jekyll-theme-minima` | installs Jekyll |
| `jekyll new website --skip-bundle` | makes a new blog in `website/` |
| `jekyll serve` | builds it and previews it at <http://127.0.0.1:4000/> |
| Ctrl-C | stops the preview server |
| `jekyll build` | builds the site into `_site/` |
| `scp -r _site/* user@host:public_html/` | copies the built site to the server |
| `ssh user@host` | a shell on the server |
| `exit` | back to your own machine |

And the files:

| File | What it is |
|------|------------|
| `_config.yml` | site settings - title, description, `baseurl` |
| `_posts/YYYY-MM-DD-name.markdown` | one blog post |
| `index.markdown`, `about.markdown` | the home page and the about page |
| `_site/` | what Jekyll builds; never edit it by hand |

The idea to carry forward: your blog is a folder of text files that a program
turns into a website. The website is not the thing you keep - the text files
are. You can rebuild the site any time, and copy it anywhere.
